params.question: A 72-year-old man on warfarin trips and strikes his head on a table. In the emergency department he is alert, oriented, GCS 15/15, with no focal neurological deficits and no vomiting. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Discharge with head injury advice — the neurological examination is normal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Age ≥65 is itself a high-risk criterion in the Canadian CT Head Rule, and any anticoagulated patient with a head injury is scanned regardless of the examination. Discharging this patient risks missing a developing extradural or subdural haematoma.

answers.text: Observe for 6 hours and scan only if he deteriorates

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Observation alone is insufficient. Both age ≥65 and anticoagulant use independently mandate an immediate CT scan. The extradural haematoma's lucid interval shows that a patient can deteriorate catastrophically during a wait-and-watch period.

answers.text: Order a non-contrast CT of the head immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Two independent high-risk criteria apply — age ≥65 and anticoagulant use. Either alone mandates immediate CT scanning per the Canadian CT Head Rule. Non-contrast CT detects blood, fractures, and mass effect rapidly without needing contrast.

answers.text: Request an MRI brain to exclude diffuse axonal injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI is reserved for suspected diffuse axonal injury (where the CT looks near-normal yet the patient remains unconscious) or for subacute findings. In acute trauma, non-contrast CT is the first-line investigation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Canadian CT Head Rule: GCS <15 at 2 hours, suspected open/depressed or basal skull fracture, ≥2 vomits, age ≥65, focal deficit, post-traumatic seizure — any one mandates CT. Anticoagulated patients are always scanned.
Well done. The Canadian CT Head Rule mandates scanning for any single high-risk feature — here, both age ≥65 and anticoagulation apply.

interactions.label: A 9-year-old girl presents with right iliac fossa pain, fever, and leucocytosis.

params.question: A 9-year-old girl presents with right iliac fossa pain, fever, and leucocytosis. The Alvarado score places her in the intermediate probability group for appendicitis. Which imaging modality is most appropriate as the first-line investigation?

answers.text: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT offers the highest sensitivity in adults and obese patients, but in a child the radiation dose makes it inappropriate as a first-line test. The ALARA principle — as low as reasonably achievable — guides imaging in paediatrics.

Correct. Ultrasound is the first-line modality for appendicitis in children, young adults, and pregnant women. It is radiation-free and can demonstrate a non-compressible appendix greater than 6 mm with surrounding fat stranding.

Plain abdominal X-rays are the first-line investigation for suspected intestinal obstruction, not appendicitis. They show air-fluid levels and dilated loops but cannot reliably visualise the appendix.
MRI is preferred in pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive. In a child, ultrasound is sufficient as the first step and avoids the sedation often required for paediatric MRI.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the ALARA principle: in children and pregnant women, ultrasound is first-line for appendicitis to minimise radiation exposure. CT follows only when ultrasound is inconclusive.
Well done. The modality is matched to the patient: ultrasound for children and pregnancy, CT for adults, MRI when ultrasound is inconclusive in pregnancy.

params.question: A CT head shows a hyperdense extra-axial collection that is crescentic in shape, crosses the coronal suture, but does not cross the midline. Which mechanism best explains these imaging characteristics?

answers.text: Arterial bleeding from the middle meningeal artery stripping the dura from the inner table

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Middle meningeal artery bleeding produces an extradural haematoma, which is biconvex (lens-shaped) and does NOT cross suture lines — the dura adheres tightly at each suture, confining the collection.

answers.text: Venous bleeding from torn bridging veins spreading in the subdural space

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A crescentic collection that crosses sutures but respects the midline falx is a subdural haematoma. Bridging veins tear as they cross the subdural space, and blood spreads freely under the dura, stopping only at the rigid falx cerebri between the hemispheres.

answers.text: Haemorrhagic contusion of the brain parenchyma at the frontal and temporal poles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Contusions are intra-parenchymal — they appear as patchy hyperdense foci within the brain tissue itself, classically at coup-contrecoup sites, not as an extra-axial crescentic collection.

answers.text: Traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage tracking along the cerebral sulci

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Subarachnoid haemorrhage fills the sulci and basal cisterns, producing a different pattern from the smooth crescentic extra-axial collection described here, which is characteristic of a subdural haematoma.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: extradural = biconvex (lens-shaped), does not cross sutures, arterial (MMA). Subdural = crescentic, crosses sutures freely, stops at the midline falx, venous (bridging veins).

Well done. The biconvex-versus-crescentic distinction is the single most clinically useful rule in trauma neuroimaging: EDH = biconvex, stops at sutures; SDH = crescentic, crosses sutures, stops at the falx.

params.question: On contrast-enhanced CT, pneumatosis intestinalis confirms bowel ischaemia before any change in bowel-wall enhancement becomes visible.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Bowel-wall enhancement is the single most important and earliest sign of viability — viable bowel enhances, ischaemic bowel does not. Pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas are late confirmatory signs, not early ones.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Absent bowel-wall enhancement is the earliest and most important CT sign of ischaemia. Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the bowel wall) and portal venous gas are late confirmatory signs that appear after the bowel has already lost viability.

params.question: A contrast-enhanced CT in a patient with a strangulated inguinal hernia shows a trapped bowel loop with absent bowel-wall enhancement. The emergency physician suggests repeating the CT in 6 hours to confirm non-viability before committing to surgery. Why is this approach not justified?

answers.text: CT scanning is contraindicated once a strangulated hernia has been diagnosed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT is appropriate in equivocal presentations and to assess bowel viability. The problem here is not the modality but the delay — the scan has already provided the answer.

answers.text: Absent bowel-wall enhancement already indicates non-viable bowel; delaying surgery risks perforation and peritonitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Absent enhancement means the bowel has lost its blood supply and is non-viable. The management pathway is emergency surgery with probable resection. Every hour of delay increases the risk of perforation, faecal peritonitis, and sepsis.

answers.text: Bowel-wall enhancement never changes over time, so a repeat scan would show identical findings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Enhancement can change — initially viable bowel may lose its blood supply with prolonged strangulation. The reason delay is wrong is that non-viable bowel needs immediate resection, not that the findings are static.

answers.text: Ultrasound, not repeat CT, is the correct follow-up investigation for assessing bowel viability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While bedside ultrasound is useful for initial groin assessment, the issue is not which modality to use next. The CT has already answered the management question: the bowel is dead and the patient needs the operating theatre.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the unifying principle: imaging does not merely label — it sizes, locates, and assesses viability, each observation mapping to a specific decision. Absent bowel-wall enhancement means dead bowel, which mandates emergency surgery with resection.
Well done. Imaging answers the surgeon's management question: absent enhancement = non-viable bowel = emergency resection. Once the answer is clear, acting on it is the priority.
